questions.q: A command table is typed Record<string, (...args: any[]) => string>. What does that cost?
questions.explain: The handlers' parameter types only protect direct calls. Through a table typed with any[], the compiler checks nothing, so mistakes turn into wrong results at runtime, such as a refund of ₦NaN.
options: Nothing; each handler still checks its own parameters at every call
Calls through the table are not checked: swapped, missing or extra arguments all compile, because any[] accepts anything
Handlers can no longer declare parameter types

questions.q: Which call compiles?
questions.explain: Only the overload signatures are visible to callers. The implementation signature would accept the other calls, but it is hidden. A union argument matches no single overload, and every overload needs three arguments.

questions.q: Callers of charge usually hold the method as a "card" | "transfer" union from a form. What is the better design?
questions.explain: Overloads never split a union across signatures. A discriminated union argument keeps each method paired with its details, and callers holding a union of payment requests can pass it directly.
options: Add more overloads until every union is covered
One signature taking a discriminated union argument, such as charge({ method: "card", card, amountKobo })

questions.q: What is the type of customer?
questions.explain: Overloads are tried from top to bottom and the first one that fits wins. The general signature matches 7, so the specific one below it is never chosen. Put specific overloads first.
options: A compile error: the overloads conflict

questions.q: find has two overloads: (id: string): Order | undefined then (ids: string[]): Order[]. What is ReturnType<typeof find>?
questions.explain: ReturnType and Parameters are conditional types with infer, and infer only sees the last overload. Name the type you need directly instead.

questions.q: Which type describes a function that formats kobo and has a currency property?
questions.explain: An object type with a call signature describes a callable value that can also have properties. In the first option, the & binds to the return type, so it describes a function returning string & { currency: string }.

questions.q: Why does Object.assign(format, { currency, symbol }) fit a MoneyFormatter type with a call signature and two properties?
questions.explain: The result type is typeof format & { currency: string; symbol: string }: callable, and with both properties, which is exactly what the interface asks for.
options: Because it returns its first argument with the properties added, typed as the intersection of the function type and the properties object
Because it creates a new class
Because functions are compatible with every object type

questions.q: What does an object type with two call signatures describe?
questions.explain: { (id: string): Order | undefined; (ids: readonly string[]): Order[] } is how overloads are written as a type, for example for a parameter that receives an overloaded function.
options: Two functions stored in one object
A function that must be called twice

questions.q: A registry stores payment gateway classes, to create instances by name later. Which type fits an element?
questions.explain: A construct signature describes something you call with new. PaymentGateway is the instance type, a call signature cannot be used with new, and an interface has no typeof because it is not a value.

questions.q: How can a construct signature type also require a static provider property on the class?
questions.explain: Static members belong to the class value, so they appear next to the construct signature, not on the instance type. A class with static readonly provider = "paystack" then fits by shape.
options: It cannot; static members are not part of any type
Write it as an object type: { new (secretKey: string): PaymentGateway; readonly provider: string }
Add static provider: string to the PaymentGateway interface

questions.q: Why does const creatable: new () => Gateway = Gateway; fail when Gateway is an abstract class?
questions.explain: A function that only inspects classes (for instanceof checks or metadata) should accept abstract new (…) => T, which both abstract and concrete classes fit.
options: Because abstract classes cannot be used as values at all
Because a normal construct signature promises that new works, and an abstract class cannot be instantiated; abstract new () => Gateway accepts it
Because abstract classes have no constructor
Because the constructor must take a parameter

questions.q: What happens to this: Cart in add(this: Cart, sku: string) when the code is compiled?
questions.explain: A this parameter exists only for the checker, which uses it to reject calls where this would be wrong. Nothing checks at runtime.
options: It becomes the first real parameter
It is erased; the compiled function has one parameter, sku
It is turned into a bind call
It becomes a runtime check that throws if this is wrong

questions.q: With add(this: Cart, sku: string) declared on cart, which line is a compile error?
questions.explain: A detached call has no object before the dot, so this is void: TS2684. call and bind supply the object explicitly.

questions.q: Why is setTimeout(cart.add, 0, "MUG-07") not reported, even though add declares this: Cart?
questions.explain: The method is passed as a value to a parameter whose type says nothing about this, so there is nothing to compare. At runtime, this is wrong. Bind the method or wrap it in an arrow function when passing it on.
options: Because setTimeout's callback type does not declare this, and the check only works where both sides mention it
Because timers run in a different realm
Because the extra argument is ignored

questions.q: What is OmitThisParameter<typeof describe>?
questions.explain: It removes the this parameter and keeps the rest, which is exactly the type of describe.bind(someProduct). ThisParameterType would give the object type.

questions.q: What is the type of refund1042?
questions.explain: Matching refund against (first: F, ...rest: A) => R captures the remaining parameters as the tuple [amountKobo: number, reason: string], labels included.
options: (orderId: string, amountKobo: number, reason: string) => string

questions.q: What is the return type of concat for concat(["ORD-7", 900] as const, [true] as const)?
questions.explain: A tuple type can spread other tuple types. Each position of both inputs is kept, in order. Without as const, the inputs would be arrays and the result an array too.

questions.q: Why does skus.map((sku) => sku.toLowerCase()) compile, when map passes three arguments to its callback?
questions.explain: Ignoring arguments is always safe, so TypeScript allows callbacks with fewer parameters. The reverse, a callback that needs more parameters than it will be given, is an error.
options: Because map is special-cased by the compiler
Because a function that takes fewer parameters can always stand in for one that is given more: it simply ignores the extra arguments
Because arrow functions have no fixed parameter count

questions.q: forEach expects a callback returning void. Why is skus.forEach((sku) => labels.push(sku)) allowed, although push returns a number?
questions.explain: This rule exists so one-line arrow callbacks work. It applies to function types; a function declared with : void itself must still not return a value.
options: Because void and number are the same type
Because a void return type in a callback type means "the caller will not use the result", so a function returning anything fits
Because arrow functions without braces always return void
It is not allowed; it is a compile error

questions.q: Under strict, which assignment is refused?
questions.explain: Parameters are contravariant: a replacement must accept at least what the original accepted. A handler for any payment can handle card events, but a card-only handler would be given bank transfers too.

questions.q: interface Notifier { notify(event: OrderEvent): void } accepts a notifier whose notify only takes ShippedEvent. Why?
questions.explain: Method bivariance is kept for compatibility with many built-in types, and it is unsound. Write the member as a property, notify: (event: OrderEvent) => void, to get the strict check.
options: Because ShippedEvent extends OrderEvent, so it is safe
Because parameters of method signatures are checked bivariantly; only function-typed properties get the strict contravariant check
Because interfaces are not checked under strict

questions.q: Which type accepts every function, including (orderId: string) => string, without using any?
questions.explain: With contravariant parameters, a function needing a string cannot accept unknown arguments. never is assignable to every parameter type, so every function fits. Calling such a function then requires a cast, which is where you promise the arguments are right.

questions.q: Why should you avoid the built-in Function type for "any function"?
questions.explain: Function behaves like an untyped callable. Use (...args: never) => unknown to accept any function, and a precise signature wherever you call it.
options: It does not exist in strict mode
It accepts calls with any arguments and returns any, so neither side of the call is checked
It cannot be used as a parameter type

questions.q: In the router's command({ usage, parse, run }), why is parse written before run?
questions.explain: Producer before consumer. If run came first, its parameters would be checked while A was still unknown.
options: Because the router calls parse first at runtime
Because A is inferred from parse's return type, and context-sensitive functions in an object literal are processed in order; run needs A for its parameters
Because object properties must be in alphabetical order
It does not matter in any way

questions.q: What protects router.exec("/refund 500000 ORD-1042") from refunding the wrong thing?
questions.explain: Text from a chat is a runtime string the compiler never sees. The typed run path protects calls written in code; parse is the only protection for text.
options: The compiler, because run's parameters are typed
The command's parse function, which validates the text at runtime and returns a usage message
Nothing; text commands cannot be checked

questions.explain: map passes the index as the second argument, and parseInt's second parameter is the radix: base 0 means "decide yourself" (10), base 1 is invalid (NaN), and "10" in base 2 is 2. Both parameters are numbers, so the types allow it. Pass a small arrow function instead of a function with optional parameters.

questions.explain: A callable object is still a function, so typeof says "function". The rate property is assigned before vat is called, so the calculation uses it: 7.5% of 2,000,000 kobo.

questions.explain: The registry holds classes, found by their static provider. new Chosen(…) works because the element type has a construct signature. Class names and provider values are different things.

questions.q: Class methods have no declared this parameter, so this compiles. What does it print?
questions.explain: The detached prototype method runs with this undefined (modules are strict), so reading this.items throws a TypeError. The arrow-function property captured this when the object was created, so it still works when detached.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Later calls return the first result without calling the function again, whatever arguments they pass. For a payment that must happen at most once, that is the point; for other uses, surprising results like this are why once should be used deliberately.

questions.q: Finish once(fn): the returned function has the same parameters and result as fn, runs fn on the first call, and returns the first result on every later call. The program should print receipt ORD-1 receipt ORD-1 1.
questions.explain: The generic rest parameter A keeps the parameter list, so sendReceipt still requires an order id. A separate done flag works even when fn returns undefined.

questions.q: Finish bindFirst(fn, first): it returns a function that takes the remaining parameters and calls fn with first in front. The program should print refund 5000 on ORD-1042: damaged.
questions.explain: Spreading rest after first matches the pattern (first: F, ...rest: A), so no cast is needed. The starter's cast compiled and passed the arguments in the wrong positions: another reason to distrust casts.

questions.q: Finish makeFormatter so it returns a callable object: calling it formats kobo as symbol + amount with two decimals, and it has currency and symbol properties. The program should print $19.99 USD $.
questions.explain: Object.assign adds the properties to the function itself and returns it, typed as the function and the properties together, which matches the call signature and both properties.

questions.q: Finish createGateway(provider, key): find the class in the registry by its static provider, throw new Error("no gateway called NAME") if there is none, and return a new instance. The program should print paystack charged 5000 then Error: no gateway called stripe.
questions.explain: The element type's construct signature is what allows new GatewayType(key), and its provider property is the class's static field. Throwing for an unknown provider is better than falling back to a default gateway silently.
questions.expected:
paystack charged 5000
Error: no gateway called stripe

questions.explain: Wrapping the call in an arrow function keeps cart before the dot, so this is right. forEach(cart.add.bind(cart)) also works. The arrow version also stops forEach's extra arguments (index and array) from reaching add.
